output.best_reason: Version B has the most distinct voice: Girard is proud, defensive and sardonic ("I am a man who sells watches"), and his trade gives him a particular way of talking about time. It builds tension through small pressures, such as the inspector's "You kept your watch in your hand," and it delivers the timings as things Girard is boasting about rather than as a list. Its closing plea about the old man's four years of work gives the character an unexpected dignity. Version A is close behind, with the tightest control of the three clean contenders and a cold, precise Girard. Version E is clean and well paced but a little thinner in texture. Version C has warmth and good beats, but its contractions and "It's a terrible thing" pull it toward modern speech and away from period feel. Version D is last because it opens with a note to the editor ("I kept the piano line...") that is not part of the interview, which is a serious flaw in a manuscript meant to be read as fiction, even though its Girard is strong.
